# Integration Relaunch: People & Organization Plan
### A reset at Month 6 — framed as a relaunch, not a rescue

---

## 0. What I think is actually happening

A short observation before the plan, because the diagnosis determines almost everything that follows.

The visible symptoms — unresolved duplicates, poaching, slow decisions, no synergy capture — are usually read as an execution failure. I'd suggest they're a *design vacuum*. Nobody has said who decides what. In the absence of decision rights, two things happen predictably: people default to their legacy process (safe), and the ambitious ones leave (they can read a stalled system faster than any dashboard can).

So the binding constraint isn't cost. It's **ambiguity**. Every week of ambiguity is costing roughly:

- 1–2% of the target's top decile in attrition (compounding, and it's the self-directed people who go first — exactly the ones a merged company needs)
- decision cycle times that have likely doubled
- the synergy case sliding right, which will eventually be read by the board as a competence question rather than a timing question

The good news, if you want to call it that: ambiguity is cheap to fix relative to almost any other problem. It requires courage more than money.

One more read worth naming out loud. Six months of drift has taught the organization that *nothing gets decided*. That belief is now the primary asset you're working against. A relaunch has to break it visibly, early, and in a way that costs somebody something — otherwise it will be filed as another announcement.

---

## 1. Design principles

These are the commitments I'd make publicly, because they constrain the plan in useful ways and let people predict behaviour without being told.

1. **Decision rights before org charts.** Structure follows clarity, not the reverse.
2. **Merit over provenance.** No fixed acquirer/target quotas. But we publish the outcome mix, because unexamined bias always favours the acquirer, and everyone will be counting anyway.
3. **Standardize the spine, free the limbs.** A short, defensible list of things that must be one way. Everything else is deliberately, unapologetically local.
4. **Speed with a decay clock.** Every open question gets a date and a default. If the date passes, the default fires automatically. Indecision becomes the expensive option.
5. **Announce in waves, complete each wave.** No partial reveals. Ambiguity is more damaging than bad news.
6. **The integration office has an expiry date.** Day 300. Written into its charter. Temporary structures that outlive their purpose become the bureaucracy you just merged to escape.
7. **Autonomy is a retention instrument.** Probably a stronger one than cash for the people you're currently losing.

---

## 2. Target operating model

### 2.1 The prior question: what kind of deal is this?

A 15% overhead commitment says cost. Two similar-sized firms in the same industry says scale and consolidation. But the talent flight says you cannot run a pure cost integration without destroying the revenue base you paid for.

**Recommended thesis: cost-led at the centre, growth-protected at the edge.** Take the overhead reduction almost entirely from corporate and shared functions, layers, spans, and duplicated infrastructure. Take very little of it from customer-facing and product-creating roles in year one. This is not sentimentality; it's where the 15% actually lives.

### 2.2 The model

**A federated model with a deliberately thin, genuinely powerful centre.**

| Layer | What it is | What it controls |
|---|---|---|
| **Centre (thin)** | ~ CEO, CFO, CHRO, GC, CIO/CTO, Strategy/Integration | Capital allocation, M&A, financial reporting and controls, legal/regulatory/risk, data & core systems spine, talent architecture (levels, pay bands, succession), brand architecture. Roughly 8–12 decisions. |
| **Business units (fat, accountable)** | 3–5 units on the clearest customer/market logic — *not* on legacy-company lines | Full P&L. Pricing within corridors, go-to-market, product roadmap, hiring within envelope, local process design, org design below Layer 3. |
| **Shared services (scale, contested)** | Transaction processing, IT infrastructure, procurement, facilities, payroll, some marketing ops | Runs to an SLA with published unit costs. BUs get a formal escalation path if service fails; that pressure is what keeps shared services honest. |
| **Communities of practice (fluid)** | Cross-cutting guilds: engineering, sales excellence, finance business partnering | No headcount, no budget authority. Set standards, move talent, spread what works. This is where the merged company actually knits together. |

**Deliberate choices embedded here:**

- **Business units are drawn on market logic, not heritage.** If you draw them on legacy company lines you have created a holding company and permanently postponed the merger. Every BU should have leadership and staff from both sides, structurally. This is the single most important structural decision in the plan.
- **The centre is small but has teeth.** The failure mode of the process-driven parent is a large centre with diffuse authority — expensive *and* slow. Fewer decisions held centrally, held absolutely.
- **Layers and spans are policy, not outcome.** Target: maximum 7 layers CEO to front line; average manager span ≥7; no people-manager with <5 reports without written exception. Publish it. This single mechanism delivers a large share of the 15% without a single subjective judgment about individuals, and it is far easier to defend as fair.

### 2.3 Where the founder-led model should *win*

Worth being explicit, because it will be watched more closely than any memo. Select two or three domains — likely customer onboarding, product iteration cadence, and hiring — and adopt the acquired firm's approach for the whole company, on the record, with a legacy-target leader owning it.

The stated reason is that it's better. The real function is signalling: merit determines outcomes, not who wrote the cheque. Nothing else you can say will land with the acquired population as convincingly, and nothing will do more to slow the poaching.

---

## 3. Restoring decision speed — the first 21 days

This runs ahead of the org design and is the highest-return work in the plan.

**Step 1: Decision inventory (Days 1–7).** Pull the 40–60 decisions that actually consume the company's time and are currently stuck: pricing exceptions, capex above threshold, hiring approvals, discount authority, product scope, vendor selection, credit terms, customer escalations.

**Step 2: Assign each one a single accountable owner** using a lightweight RAPID/DACI. One name in the "decide" box. Not a committee. Not "jointly."

**Step 3: Publish the Decision Charter** — one document, publicly accessible, showing every decision, its owner, its authority limit, and its SLA (e.g. pricing exceptions: 48 hours). Anyone in the company can look up who decides.

**Step 4: Apply an interim rule while the rest is designed** — *"Where no charter entry exists, the process of the business unit that owns the customer relationship applies."* Bias to action, bias to the customer, and it stops the "whose process?" question from consuming another quarter.

**Step 5: Open a Decision Debt Register.** Anyone can post a stuck decision. Every entry gets an owner and a date within 72 hours. Review it weekly in the executive meeting, publish the ageing. Visibility does most of the work; nobody wants to be the oldest item on the list.

**Step 6: Cut the meeting estate.** Cancel every recurring cross-company meeting created since close. Re-establish only those with a named owner, a decision purpose, and an end date. You'll likely recover 15–20% of management capacity, which you need for the next 100 days.

*Rough expectation: decision cycle time back to pre-deal levels within six weeks, and it's measurable — sample 20 decision types, measure request-to-resolution, publish the trend.*

---

## 4. Leader selection and duplicate role resolution

### 4.1 The cascade

Selection runs top-down, one layer at a time, each layer complete before the next begins. Each layer's newly confirmed leaders staff the layer below them, with HR and one cross-company panel member — this transfers ownership into the line quickly and stops the integration office from becoming the permanent arbiter of everyone's career.

| Layer | Population | Design done | Selection done | Announced |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| L1 – Exec (CEO-1) | ~10 | Already or Day 10 | Day 20 | Day 21 |
| L2 – Function/BU leads | ~40–60 | Day 25 | Day 40 | Day 42 |
| L3 – Senior managers | ~150–250 | Day 45 | Day 65 | Day 70 |
| L4 – Managers | ~500–800 | Day 70 | Day 95 | Day 100 |
| L5+ – Individual contributors | Remainder | Day 95 | Day 125 | Day 130 |

Whole layers announced on a single day. Consultation/works council requirements will vary by jurisdiction; run those in parallel from Day 1 and let the legal calendar set the announcement dates, not the reverse.

**One hundred and thirty days from relaunch to complete clarity.** That is the promise. It is aggressive, and it should be — the cost of a slower, "more careful" process is now higher than the cost of a few imperfect placements. Imperfect placements are correctable. The people leaving are not.

### 4.2 How selection is actually made

**Slate, then select.** For every role, build a slate from both firms plus (for L1–L2) an external benchmark candidate. Everyone competes; nobody is grandfathered. Incumbency is not a qualification.

**Scorecard, weighted and published in advance:**

| Criterion | Weight | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Delivery against the future role's outcomes | 35% | Not past-role performance. The job is changing. |
| Capability fit to the target operating model | 25% | Especially: operating with ambiguity, deciding without full information |
| Leadership behaviours / builds followership across both heritages | 25% | Evidenced, not asserted |
| Institutional knowledge critical to continuity | 15% | Real value, genuinely time-limited — decays over ~18 months |

**Fairness mechanics that matter more than the scorecard:**

- **Mixed panels.** No selection decision made by a panel drawn from one legacy company. Ever.
- **Independent assessment at L1–L2.** External assessors, structured, same instrument for both sides. Costly, and worth it — it's the only credible answer to "the acquirer just picked its own people."
- **Calibration on provenance.** After each layer, look at the outcome mix. If a function is placing 80% from one heritage, that isn't automatically wrong, but it demands an articulated explanation before sign-off. Bias rarely announces itself.
- **Published outcome data.** Selection ratios by heritage, gender, ethnicity, level, after each wave. Companies that hide this number are always assumed to be hiding something worse than the truth.
- **A real appeal route.** 10 working days, reviewed by a panel excluding the original deciders. Expect it to overturn very little — that isn't its purpose. Its purpose is that the process is *seen* to have a check on it.

### 4.3 Outcomes for those not selected

Three doors, offered in this order:

1. **Redeployment** — first refusal on open roles at level for 60 days, plus a genuine internal marketplace (see §5). Target 20–30% of displaced managers redeployed; it protects capability and it is far cheaper than severance plus re-hire.
2. **Transition with dignity** — severance above statutory, extended vesting where defensible, outplacement, 90-day working notice where practical, alumni network access. How you treat leavers is the loudest signal available to those who stay, and the second-loudest to the market you'll be recruiting from next year.
3. **Bridge roles** — time-boxed, clearly labelled, real work (integration workstream lead, knowledge transfer, customer transition). Never a disguised holding pattern; people see through it and it corrodes trust in everything else you say.

### 4.4 A note on the founder

This needs resolving in the first 21 days, not the first 21 weeks.

A founder in an undefined post-merger role is the most destabilizing single variable available — an alternative power centre that people route around the formal structure to reach. There are two honourable outcomes: a **defined mandate with real authority** (a business unit, a growth agenda, a product franchise — with a P&L and a place in the Decision Charter), or a **clean, well-honoured exit** with public thanks and clear terms on what they will and won't do next.

Both work. The middle — "advisor," "vice chair," "helping with culture" — does not. If a founder-led exit is chosen, expect a retention wave to follow within 60 days and pre-fund the response.

---

## 5. Retaining critical talent

Retention has been leaking for six months. Assume some of the best people already have offers in hand.

### 5.1 Define "critical" properly

Top performance ratings are a poor proxy. Segment on **replacement difficulty × business impact**:

| Segment | Typical size | Approach |
|---|---|---|
| **Irreplaceable** — key customer relationships, unique technical depth, single points of institutional knowledge | 1–2% | Bespoke, CEO/L1-level engagement, within 14 days |
| **Scarce** — hard-to-hire skills, deep domain expertise, integration-critical | 5–8% | Structured retention package + role clarity, within 30 days |
| **Emerging** — high trajectory, will define the company in 3–5 years | 3–5% | Development, visibility, sponsorship — often responds better to opportunity than money |
| **Steady core** | Remainder | Retained by clarity, fair process, and a functioning manager — which is to say, by everything else in this plan |

Build the list with mixed-heritage input. Manager nominations alone will systematically under-identify people from the acquired firm.

### 5.2 What to actually do — in the first 30 days

**Re-recruit, individually.** Every person in the top two segments gets a face-to-face conversation with a leader who matters, covering: your role in the new company, why you specifically, what you'll own, and what the next two years could look like. Not a retention letter. A conversation. Roughly 200–400 conversations in 30 days; it's the highest-return use of executive time available right now.

**Financial instruments, used surgically:**
- 12–24 month retention awards, 50% at 12 months / 50% at 24 (or on milestone completion, which is better where milestones are real)
- Equity refresh for the Irreplaceable and Scarce segments — particularly acquired-firm employees whose original equity story ended at close and who currently have no forward-looking upside at all. This is a common and expensive oversight.
- Immediate spot correction of pay inversions between heritages in the same role. Salary transparency is functionally universal now; discovered inequity does more damage than the cost of fixing it.

Budget guide: **1.0–1.5% of the combined payroll**, front-loaded. Compare against the cost of replacing a top performer at 1.5–2.0× salary plus revenue disruption, and it's not a close call.

**Non-financial instruments, which for this population are probably stronger:**
- **Ownership.** Give the best people a franchise — a product, a segment, a market — with real authority in the Decision Charter and a clear line to results. Self-directed people leave because they've lost the ability to act, not because of pay. Pay is the reason they give in the exit interview.
- **An internal talent marketplace.** Post every open role internally first, for 10 days, visible to everyone. Let people move toward the work that interests them. It undercuts the poachers on their strongest argument — "you're stuck" — and it surfaces capability the org chart never would.
- **Speed of resolution.** The single most effective retention act available is telling people what their job is. Everything in §4 is a retention programme.

**Counter-offer policy.** Decide it now, centrally, and hold it. Ad hoc counter-offers create a market where resignation is the fastest route to a raise, and word travels within days. Approved exceptions only, at L1 level, logged.

**Instrument the leak.** Weekly regretted-attrition tracking by heritage, function, and critical segment. Track *external recruiter contact rates* too — via pulse survey, and honestly, via what your leaders hear. It's a leading indicator with about a 6–10 week lead on actual resignations.

---

## 6. Process standardization: what's the spine, what's a limb

The "best of both" approach sounds fair and reliably produces paralysis — it invites 400 separate negotiations. Replace it with a triage and a clock.

### 6.1 The test

Standardize only where at least one is true:

1. **Regulatory, financial control, or risk** — no discretion available
2. **The customer sees it** and must see one company (contracts, pricing architecture, service commitments, brand)
3. **Real scale economics** — the unit cost genuinely falls with volume (procurement, payroll, infrastructure, transaction processing)
4. **It's the data spine** — chart of accounts, customer master, employee master, product hierarchy. Without one version of these you cannot manage, report, or even verify the synergy case
5. **It blocks talent mobility** — levels, titles, pay bands, performance cycles. Without these, people can't move between units, and the merger stays notional

Otherwise: **leave it alone.** Explicitly, publicly, with a named owner. Deliberate difference is a decision, not an oversight — and saying so removes the anxiety that drives people to standardize things nobody asked them to.

### 6.2 Illustrative triage

| Standardize now (Days 1–120) | Standardize later (Days 120–365) | Deliberately different | Stop doing |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chart of accounts, financial close | ERP consolidation | Sales methodology by segment | Duplicate committees |
| Delegation of authority | HRIS single instance | Product development cadence | Legacy board reporting packs |
| Job architecture, levels, pay bands | Procurement categories (waves) | Local marketing execution | Overlapping approval gates |
| Customer & employee master data | CRM consolidation | Service delivery models by market | Duplicate vendor management |

# Legacy Platform End-of-Life & Migration Program

**Program name:** *Bridge* — a 42-month, gated transition of Platform L (legacy) to Platform N (current).

> **Working assumptions** (replace with your actuals; the structure holds either way): Platform L generates ~35% of profit across ~4,000 customers; the top ~40 accounts represent ~55% of L revenue; sustaining cost is ~$25–30M/yr growing 10–15%; 6–10 engineers hold irreplaceable L knowledge, 4 within 3 years of retirement.

---

## 1. The core strategic call

Three things are true simultaneously and the plan must respect all of them:

1. **You cannot keep L.** Cost curve compounds, the knowledge base is evaporating, and unpatched exposure is an existential (not financial) risk. Time is not neutral — waiting is the expensive option.
2. **You cannot force-march the top accounts.** They are a third of your profit and they have credible alternatives. A migration they experience as coercion converts a support problem into a competitive loss.
3. **"Feature parity" is the wrong goal.** *Job parity* is the goal. You must rebuild the outcomes a handful of loyal customers actually depend on — and you must be ruthless about the long tail of toggles nobody uses.

**Therefore the operating principle:** *fixed dates, negotiable paths.* The sunset calendar is published once and never slips. What *is* flexible — generously so — is the route each customer takes to get there, who pays for it, and what a paid, priced, per-account extension looks like at the tail.

**Second principle — no surprises, no unilateral loss:** you publish the feature commitments *before* you publish the shutoff date, and you accept contractual remedies if you miss them.

---

## 2. Phase 0 — Discovery and instrumentation (Months −6 to 0)

**Do not announce anything until this is done.** An EOL date announced without usage data and a parity commitment is how you lose your top ten accounts in one quarter.

| Workstream | Output | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| Usage telemetry / fingerprinting | Per-account, per-feature, per-API usage map for 100% of L installs (on-prem: opt-in agent, log ingest, or paid audit) | Eng + Data |
| Feature census | Every shipped capability, flag, endpoint, report, format, connector — with active-user counts | Product |
| Account segmentation & risk scoring | Tiering + defection risk model (§8) | Sales Ops + CS |
| Cost-of-carry model | True annual L cost incl. security, infra, opportunity cost of engineers, insurance loading | Finance |
| Knowledge asset audit | Which subsystems have exactly one human who understands them | Eng leadership |
| Legal review | Contract-by-contract: perpetual licenses, support commitments, OEM/embedded rights, regulated-industry obligations, notice periods | Legal |
| Competitive intel | Rival migration offers, switching-cost model, likely poaching targets | Product Marketing |

**Critical gate:** you cannot set a credible calendar without knowing *which 40 features are load-bearing for which 200 customers*. Expect the surprise: typically 70–85% of L's feature surface has effectively zero active users, while 3–6 obscure capabilities are individually worth 8-figure relationships.

## 3. Sunset timeline and support policy

### 3.1 Support lifecycle states

Publish these as a formal, versioned policy document — this becomes the contractual reference.

| State | What you get | What you don't |
|---|---|---|
| **Full Support** (now → M18) | Bug fixes, security patches, OS/DB/browser compatibility updates, standard SLAs, migration-blocker fixes | New features (frozen at M0) |
| **Maintenance Support** (M18 → M30) | Security patches, Sev-1/Sev-2 bug fixes, existing-platform compatibility only | New compatibility certifications, Sev-3/4 fixes, enhancements |
| **Extended Security Support** — paid uplift (M30 → M42) | Critical/High CVE remediation only, Sev-1 workarounds, best-effort response | Bug fixes, compatibility, standard SLAs |
| **Custom Support Agreement** — bespoke, per-account (M42 → M54 max) | Negotiated scope, capped, priced at 2.5–3× original maintenance, minimum 12-month commitment, minimum contract value | Anything not explicitly enumerated |
| **End of Life** (M42 public / M54 absolute) | Nothing. Hosted instances decommissioned; on-prem software may run at customer's own risk with signed liability acknowledgment | — |

### 3.2 The calendar

| Milestone | Timing | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Confidential briefings, top 40 + OEMs** | M−1 | 3–4 weeks ahead of public, under NDA, exec-to-exec |
| **Public announcement** — full calendar, parity commitments, incentives, tooling roadmap | **M0** | Single coordinated moment: customers, partners, analysts, field, press |
| **End of Sale** — no new L customers | M0 | Immediate |
| **End of Expansion** — no new seats/capacity/modules on L | M12 | Grandfather in-flight projects case-by-case to M18 |
| **Feature freeze** (except adjudicated migration blockers) | M0 | Blocker exception process is the trust mechanism |
| **Parity Wave 1 GA** on Platform N | M9 | Highest-value rebuilt capabilities |
| **Migration tooling GA** (assessment + converter + parallel-run) | M9 | Must precede any pressure campaign |
| **Parity Wave 2 GA** | M15 | Completes committed rebuild scope |
| **Full Support ends → Maintenance Support** | M18 | |
| **Scale migration window** | M12–M30 | ~65% of accounts should cut over here |
| **Standard support ends** | **M30** | Extended Security Support begins, priced at 1.5× (M30–36), 2.0× (M36–42) |
| **Extended support ends; hosted decommission begins** | **M42** | |
| **Absolute EOL / hard stop** | **M54** | Custom Support Agreements only; nothing beyond |

**Runway rationale:** 30 months of standard support gives even a heavily customized enterprise two budget cycles and two change-freeze-free windows. 42 months total is defensible to auditors and regulators. Beyond that, escalating price does the persuading rather than escalating threats.

### 3.3 The security tripwire (state this up front, at M0)

Publish a named exception: *if an unpatchable Critical vulnerability appears in an out-of-support dependency, we will accelerate specific end-dates with 90 days' notice.* Saying this on day one converts a future betrayal into a pre-agreed, jointly understood condition — and it gives your CISO a legitimate lever instead of a fight.

## 4. Feature triage: rebuild vs. bridge vs. retire

### 4.1 Decision framework

Score every candidate capability (0–5 each):

- **A. Revenue dependency** — ARR of accounts that would be blocked without it
- **B. Obligation** — regulatory, contractual, or audit requirement (binary multiplier: if yes, rebuild)
- **C. Substitutability** — is there an acceptable workaround, partner product, API, or services path?
- **D. Strategic fit** — does it belong in N's architecture, or would it import legacy debt?
- **E. Rebuild cost** — engineering months, ongoing maintenance drag

| Outcome | Trigger | Commitment level |
|---|---|---|
| **Rebuild native** | High A, or B=yes; fits D | Named in public parity roadmap with a GA quarter and contractual remedy if missed |
| **Bridge** (compat shim, adapter, transpiler, plugin, partner) | High A, poor D — needed, but shouldn't live in the core | Shipped with *its own* sunset date (typically EOL+24m) |
| **Substitute** (services, one-time custom build, config recipe) | Moderate A, high C, low D | Funded by vendor for Tier 1/2; documented recipe for Tier 3 |
| **Retire** | Low A, high C | Named publicly with the replacement path and an appeal window |

### 4.2 Expected shape of the answer

Typically: **~10–15% rebuild, ~15% bridge, ~10% substitute, ~60–65% retire by feature count** — while the rebuild+bridge set covers **85–90% of at-risk revenue**. Say this out loud internally so nobody equates "retiring most of the feature surface" with "abandoning customers."

### 4.3 Common archetypes and the right call

| Archetype | Typical call | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Deep connector to an ancient upstream system (mainframe, legacy ERP, AS/400) | **Rebuild** as a supported connector — or **partner** with an integration specialist | It's the actual lock-in; losing it loses the account |
| Regulatory output fidelity (statutory filings, EDI, print/forms, audit trails, retention) | **Rebuild, byte-exact, with reconciliation proof** | Non-negotiable; failure here is a compliance event, not an inconvenience |
| Arcane scripting/macro/customization engine with thousands of customer-authored scripts | **Bridge**: interpreter or transpiler covering the ~top 90% of constructs; convert the rest as funded services | Rewriting customer IP by hand is where migrations die |
| Legacy v1 API / batch/CLI surface | **Bridge**: compatibility shim with its own published sunset | Buys integration partners and customer IT time |
| Exotic deployment mode (air-gapped, unsupported OS/DB, self-hosted single-tenant) | **Segment decision**: rebuild only if a coherent, priced segment exists (gov/defense/regulated); otherwise a premium Custom Support path | Don't rebuild an unfunded architecture |
| Permission/workflow model quirks, granular admin semantics | **Rebuild the semantics**, not the UI | Cheap relative to the trust it buys; blocks admin sign-off otherwise |
| Long-tail flags, deprecated report variants, sub-1% toggles | **Retire** | This is where you fund the rest |

### 4.4 The Migration Blocker Board — your single most important trust mechanism

- **Any customer, any tier, can file a "Migration Blocker."** Public intake form, no gatekeeping by account size.
- **15-business-day adjudication SLA.** Four verdicts: *Rebuild (with quarter)*, *Bridge*, *Workaround (documented, validated with the customer)*, *Won't fix (with reasoning)*.
- **Public register** — all filings, status, verdicts, dates. Visible to all customers.
- **Cross-functional board**: Product (chair), Eng, CS, Sales, and a rotating customer advisory seat.
- **Reserved capacity:** hold 20–25% of the parity engineering budget unallocated for blockers discovered after M0. They *will* arrive, and refusing them is what breaks the program's credibility.

The register converts "you're abandoning us" into "there is a visible, fair process, and my issue is #47 with a Q3 date." That shift is worth more than any discount.

---

Treat this as a funded product with a PM, a roadmap, and its own SLAs. Under-tooling is the single most common cause of EOL programs slipping.

| Component | Purpose | Target |
|---|---|---|
| **Readiness Assessment / "Migration Passport"** | Auto-generated per-account report: features used, blockers, effort estimate, recommended path, custom code inventory | M6 |

# People & Organization Integration Plan — Post-Merger Reset

**Working assumption:** "Meridian" (process-driven, hierarchical, legal acquirer) and "Kestrel" (informal, founder-led). Combined ~5,200 FTE, ~$1.8B revenue, addressable overhead base ~$520M → **15% = ~$78M run-rate synergy**. Illustrative figures; the architecture holds at any scale.

---

## 0. The Reset Thesis: Five Decisions Made Now

Six months of ambiguity has produced a predictable pathology: no one has been told who wins, so everyone is hedging. The fix is not more analysis — it is **a small number of irreversible, publicly announced decisions**, made fast, with visible fairness.

| # | Decision | Made by |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **This is an integration, not a federation.** One operating model, one process spine, one P&L. The "merger of equals" language stops today. | Day 3 (CEO + Board) |
| 2 | **Structure: unified functions + segment-facing front end + one ring-fenced high-velocity growth unit.** Kestrel's speed is preserved in one place by design, not everywhere by accident. | Day 10 |
| 3 | **Default rule effective immediately:** where no new standard has been published, **Meridian's process applies** and the named single owner may waive it. Ambiguity ends by fiat. | Day 5 |
| 4 | **Leadership named three levels down within 45 days**, one process, one bar, published rules. No co-heads. | Day 45 |
| 5 | **One reduction event, not rolling cuts.** Design by Day 60, notifications Day 75–95 (later where consultation is required), full run-rate by Month 15. | Day 60 |

Everything below serves these five.

---

## 1. Diagnosis: What Actually Went Wrong

| Symptom | Root cause | Implication for the plan |
|---|---|---|
| Duplicate roles unresolved | No leadership cascade; "best athlete" rhetoric with no method, so no one could be deselected without accusation of bias | Need a published, defensible selection methodology before any names |
| Top performers poached | Ambiguity about role, boss, and scope is the #1 driver of voluntary exit — not pay. Founder's own role is undefined, so the loyalty network has nothing to anchor to | Retention is 70% clarity, 30% cash. Resolve the founder question first |
| Decision-making slowed | Two live governance systems, two delegation-of-authority matrices, dual approval chains, no decider of record | Decision Rights Charter is the highest-leverage two-week deliverable |
| Synergies not started | Cost targets never converted into function-level owner-baseline-milestone commitments in the budget; no IMO with teeth | Move synergy from a "case" into the forecast and into incentive plans |
| Culture friction | Treated as a values-poster exercise instead of a conflict about *how decisions get made and how much rigor is required* | Culture work must be encoded in decision rights, promotion criteria, and meeting norms |

**Cost of continued drift:** attrition in the top-performer cohort compounds at roughly 2–3x baseline; each month of delay pushes ~$6.5M of run-rate synergy out and permanently forfeits some of it as the case ages.

---

## 2. Target Operating Model

### 2.1 The design choice
Two same-industry companies of similar size means the value is in **scale and overlap elimination**, not in preserving two systems. But the acquired firm's velocity is a real asset that a hierarchical spine will kill if applied indiscriminately. The answer is deliberate asymmetry.

**"One backbone, two speeds."**

**Layer 1 — Unified corporate spine (fully consolidated, single instance, Meridian-led standards):**
Finance, HR, Legal & Compliance, IT, Procurement, Corporate Communications, Strategy/M&A. Structured as *centers of expertise + one shared-services hub* with a global process owner per end-to-end process (record-to-report, hire-to-retire, source-to-pay, quote-to-cash).

**Layer 2 — Commercial front end (segment-facing, single go-to-market):**
One sales organization organized by customer segment (not by legacy heritage), one pricing authority, one CRM, one account ownership map, one comp plan effective at the next plan year. Named account transitions are deliberately *slowed* — no top-100 account changes reps in the first 12 months absent a customer-driven reason.

**Layer 3 — Operations / delivery / supply chain:**
Consolidated on a network basis (best-site, best-process), sequenced after commercial stability. Site consolidation decisions announced with the org design so people get one shock, not three.

**Layer 4 — "Growth Engine" (the ring-fence):**
Kestrel's core innovation/new-product engine, ~200–350 people, retained as a distinct unit with:
- Different governance: a single sponsor (CEO or Chief Product Officer), quarterly funding gates instead of annual budgeting, capital allocated as venture tranches
- Different processes: light stage gates, exempt from standard procurement thresholds up to a set limit, own hiring req authority
- Different metrics: learning/velocity/pipeline value, not quarterly margin
- Consumes the backbone for payroll, security, legal, financial reporting — **no exceptions on the plumbing**
- A written charter with a 24-month review, so the ring-fence is a decision, not a permanent carve-out

**Layers and spans targets (published, enforced):** ≤7 layers CEO to front line; average span ≥8; no people manager with <5 direct reports without CEO exception. These two ratios alone typically deliver 30–40% of an overhead target.

### 2.2 What we explicitly reject
- Co-leadership / "co-heads of…" — the single largest destroyer of decision speed in mergers of equals
- Dual-brand internal identity beyond Month 12
- "Let each side keep its own systems until we pick the best" — the current state, which has cost six months
- Rolling redundancies function by function over a year

---

## 3. Restoring Decision Speed (Days 1–21, Highest Priority)

### 3.1 Decision Rights Charter (published Day 14)
Take the **top 25 recurring decisions** (pricing exceptions and discount approval, hiring reqs, capex, customer contract terms, product roadmap, marketing spend, vendor selection, org changes, comp exceptions, credit terms, quality/regulatory calls…). For each, assign **DACI**: one **Decider** (a named person, never a committee), Approver (only where legally/fiduciarily required), Contributors, Informed.

Rules of the road:
- **Single-signature rule.** Every decision has exactly one name. If you cannot name the decider, the IMO assigns one within 24 hours.
- **Default-to-Meridian rule.** Absent a published new standard, the acquirer's process applies. The named process owner may grant written waivers. This converts thousands of daily stalls into action.
- **Escalation SLA.** Unresolved at L3 → 48 hours to L2; unresolved at L2 → 5 business days to the Integration Steering Committee. Escalations are tracked; a leader with repeated escalations is coached or replaced.
- **Two-way-door presumption.** If a decision is reversible within a quarter, decide in the room with 70% information. Only genuine one-way doors (systems platform, legal entity, brand, site closures) get full analysis.

### 3.2 Harmonized Delegation of Authority (Day 21)
One DOA matrix, one signature-limit table, one purchase-approval workflow. Deliberately push limits **down** one notch versus legacy Meridian as a visible signal that integration is not bureaucratization.

### 3.3 Governance detox (Day 21)
Abolish all legacy steering committees and standing forums. Rebuild a single cadence:

| Forum | Cadence | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Executive Leadership Team | Weekly, 90 min | Operating decisions, escalations |
| Integration Steering Committee (subset of ELT + IMO lead + CFO + CHRO) | Bi-weekly, 2 hrs | Value capture, milestones, unblocking |
| Talent & Selection Calibration Board | Weekly during Days 15–90 | Leader selection, adverse-impact review, retention exceptions |
| Business reviews | Monthly | Trading performance, one format |
| Board integration update | Monthly | Synergy run-rate, attrition, risk |

**Meeting amnesty:** every recurring meeting is cancelled on Day 21 and must be re-justified by an owner with a purpose and decision output.

### 3.4 IMO with teeth (Day 7)
Replace the PMO with an **Integration Management Office** led by a full-time, credible senior executive (a respected P&L leader, ideally from the acquired side — a powerful fairness signal), reporting to the CEO, with the CFO as value-capture co-owner. Workstream leads are full-time and freed of day jobs; working teams are dual-heritage co-staffed, but every workstream has **one** lead.

---

## 4. Leadership Selection and Duplicate Role Resolution

### 4.1 The cascade (the only way to move fast and fairly)
Top-down, one level at a time, each selected leader designs and selects the level below within a fixed window.

| Level | Designed & named by |
|---|---|
| L1 (ELT direct reports to CEO) | Day 14 |
| L2 (function/business leaders, ~40 roles) | Day 30 |
| L3 (~200 roles, covers most duplication) | Day 45 |
| L4 and below | Day 60 design, Day 75–95 notifications |

Every leader receives the **same three-part brief** before selecting: (a) the org design principles and spans/layers targets, (b) their function's cost target, (c) the selection methodology and their obligation to use it.

### 4.2 Selection methodology (published to all employees before it is used)
1. **Role first, person second.** Write the new role's scorecard — accountabilities, decision rights, the 3–5 outcomes for the next 18 months, capabilities required.
2. **Slate both pools.** Every role slate must include qualified candidates from both legacy companies; a single-heritage slate requires written justification to the Calibration Board.
3. **Common bar.** Assess on (i) forward capability against the scorecard, (ii) demonstrated results, (iii) change and integration leadership — explicitly including *evidence of behavior during the last six months*, (iv) the new company's five behaviors. Legacy title, tenure, and "who I know" are excluded criteria.
4. **Cross-heritage panels.** Minimum two interviewers, never both from the same legacy company. Structured guides; written evidence-based rationale for each decision.
5. **Calibration.** Weekly Board review of all L1–L3 selections together — not role by role — to enforce a consistent bar and prevent empire-protection.
6. **Published tie-break.** Where two candidates are genuinely equivalent: prefer the candidate whose retention risk-adjusted value to the combined company is higher, then the candidate representing the under-represented heritage in that function's leadership. Stated publicly in advance so it reads as principle, not favoritism.
7. **Representation guardrail, not a quota.** Track legacy-heritage mix at L1–L3 against the ~50/50 headcount split. Material skew requires a written explanation to the CEO and Board. Target: neither heritage below ~35% at L1–L3 by Day 45. *(This is the single most-watched fairness metric by the acquired employee base.)*
8. **Adverse-impact analytics.** Every wave reviewed by HR and employment counsel across heritage, gender, ethnicity, age, disability, geography before notification.
9. **Appeal path.** An independent ombudsperson (external or a non-conflicted internal executive) hears process complaints within 5 days; can order a re-run of a selection, cannot substitute judgment on the outcome.

### 4.3 Resolving duplicate roles below leadership
- **Job architecture harmonization first (Days 1–30):** one leveling framework, one title taxonomy, one grade-to-pay-band mapping. Without this, "duplicate" cannot be defined.
- **Role mapping:** every legacy position mapped to the target design and classified as **(A) unique/direct slot-in, (B) many-to-one consolidation → competitive selection, (C) genuinely new → open internal posting, (D) eliminated.**
- **Method by class:** A = slot, no process. B = structured selection using §4.2. C = internal-only posting for 10 business days, then external. D = redeployment window.

# Legacy Sunset & Migration Program — Working Draft

*A note on how this is framed: I've written it as a set of decisions with the reasoning exposed, rather than a mandate to be approved. Most of it can be started without anyone signing anything. The two places where I'd want the room to actually stop and look at each other are marked as gates.*

---

## 1. What this program is actually about

It's tempting to treat this as a decommissioning project. I'd suggest it isn't. Decommissioning is what happens to the servers at the end. What we're actually doing is transferring a third of our profit from one platform to another *without the customer feeling transferred* — and, separately, defusing a slow-burning operational hazard (unpatched surface area, retiring institutional memory).

Two observations that shape everything below:

**The announcement is the single largest defection event in the program.** The day we publish a date is the day procurement at every large account is handed a legitimate reason to run a competitive evaluation. So the sequence matters more than the timeline. Nothing goes public until the tooling, the parity commitments, and the top-account conversations are already in motion. Announcing first and building second is the most common way this goes wrong.

**A published date that slips is worse than a longer date held.** Credibility is the currency we're spending. I'd rather commit to 42 months and beat it than commit to 24 and move it twice.

---

## 2. Phase 0 — Quiet work (Months 0–6, no external signal)

Nothing here requires telling the market anything.

**Instrument the old platform.** We are guessing about which niche features matter. That guessing is expensive. Ship lightweight feature-level telemetry (or mine logs/support tickets/config dumps where telemetry isn't feasible) and produce a single artifact: *feature × account × revenue × frequency*. This becomes the spine of every later decision.

**Contract archaeology.** Someone should read the top 50 legacy contracts properly. Specifically hunting for: perpetual license grants, evergreen support obligations, uptime/patch commitments, source escrow clauses, regulated-sector or public-sector terms, and renewal/notice dates. There will be surprises. There always are, and they tend to be the kind that turn a plan into a lawsuit.

**Knowledge capture, treated as urgent rather than important.** The retirement horizon is the hardest constraint in this whole picture — harder than the customers, because it isn't negotiable. Three moves:
- Retention agreements with the small handful of engineers who genuinely hold the model, structured against *deliverables* (recorded architecture walkthroughs, runbooks, failure catalogues, a named and demonstrably competent successor) rather than time served.
- A pairing/apprenticeship rotation. Bus factor tracked as a program metric, per subsystem.
- A standing contractor bench, engaged and warm before we need it, not after.

**Freeze and harden, don't maintain.** The cheapest way to reduce ongoing exposure is to stop changing the thing. Containerise or otherwise encapsulate the legacy stack, put it behind a modern gateway/WAF, aggressively narrow its network surface, move authentication out to the current identity layer, and reduce the patch obligation to the smallest defensible set. This converts an open-ended maintenance liability into something closer to a fixed-cost appliance — and it buys most of the time we need at a fraction of the cost of "keeping it modern."

**Prototype the assessment tool.** Before we promise migration, we should be able to point a scanner at a customer's legacy configuration and produce: an inventory of what they use, a parity gap list, an effort estimate, and a draft migration plan. This artifact does more for retention than any discount.

**Option worth keeping on the table:** divesting or spinning out the legacy line to a specialist long-tail maintenance acquirer. There's a whole industry that does exactly this. It would serve the most loyal customers better than we intend to, remove the cost curve entirely, and monetise the tail. I'm not proposing it as the primary path — but if the feature triage comes back showing an irreducible core of genuinely bespoke capability serving a handful of accounts, this is the cleaner answer, and I'd rather we discovered that in month 4 than month 30.

---

## 3. Feature triage — rebuild versus retire

I'd resist letting this become a debate about individual features. It should be a rule that anyone can apply, so the argument happens once.

**The rule:** score each legacy-only capability on (a) revenue-weighted adoption, (b) whether a workflow substitute exists in the new product, (c) strategic coherence with where the new product is going, (d) rebuild cost. Then place it in one of four buckets.

| Bucket | Criteria | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **Rebuild native** | Used by >15% of legacy revenue, or by ≥3 strategic accounts, and consistent with the new product's direction | Full first-class implementation on the roadmap, dated, funded |
| **Rebuild as compatibility layer** | Behaviour-bound rather than value-bound — customers depend on *exact* semantics (report formats, scripting/macro syntax, obscure protocols, batch-scheduling quirks) | Adapter/shim, explicitly labelled as a compatibility surface with its own eventual sunset. Contain the ugliness; don't let it into the core |
| **Partner or services** | Genuinely bespoke, one or two accounts, high cost, low strategic fit | Hand to a partner/SI, or deliver as a funded custom extension. Consider licensing the legacy module out |
| **Retire with a landing** | Trivial usage, or a superior path already exists | Retire — but never bare. Every retirement ships with a documented alternative workflow, a hands-on transition session, and where appropriate a commercial gesture |

**The discipline that makes this credible:** nothing enters "retire" without a named alternative and a named human who has walked a real customer through it. "You can achieve this another way" is not a plan; it's a support ticket waiting to happen.

**Gate 1 (end of Month 6):** the triage table, the parity roadmap with dates, and the funding for it. This is one of the two moments where I'd want genuine collective commitment, because everything external depends on it holding.

---

## 4. Sunset timeline and support policy

Dates are relative to public announcement (T0), which lands in Month 9 of internal work.

| Milestone | Timing | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| End of new sales & new deployments | T0 | No new legacy logos, no new legacy instances. Existing customers can still add capacity |
| End of feature development | T0 (formalises current reality) | Only parity-critical and security work |
| End of new platform certifications | T0 + 12m | No new OS / database / browser / dependency versions. A quiet but powerful forcing function — customers' own infrastructure cycles begin pushing them |
| End of standard support | T0 + 30m | Full SLAs, all severities, standard pricing ends here |
| End of maintenance support | T0 + 42m | Critical defects and security only, degraded SLA, uplifted pricing |
| **End of life** | **T0 + 48m** | No patches, no support. Product is unsupported |
| Extended support (by exception, named accounts) | to T0 + 60m | Security-only, contracted individually, priced to be uncomfortable |

Roughly four years to EOL, five with exceptions. Given that this is a third of profit and the loyal base is genuinely dependent, anything materially shorter creates the vendor-switching event we're trying to avoid. Anything longer and the engineering-retirement problem eats us.

**Support ladder as an incentive, not just a policy.** The pricing uplift on the legacy platform steps up — nominally 0% / +15% / +40% / +100% across the four years — *and is waived entirely for any account with a signed migration plan and demonstrable milestone progress.* The message is legible without being said aloud: standing still gets expensive; moving is free. Nobody has to be threatened.

---

## 5. Migration tooling

The tooling is the retention strategy. Discounts buy a renewal; tooling removes the fear.

- **Assessment scanner** — inventory, parity gaps, effort estimate, generated plan. Available to the customer directly, on demand.
- **Automated configuration and data converters** — settings, permissions, integrations, historical data, with a validation report. Target: 80%+ of the long tail migrating with no human from us involved.
- **Dual-run / shadow mode** — old and new operating in parallel against live data, with an output-diffing report. This is the thing that converts "we can't risk it" into "we watched it match for six weeks." Worth over-investing in.
- **Rollback path** — documented, tested, time-boxed. Customers migrate faster when retreat is cheap.
- **Compatibility bridge** — legacy integrations and API surface exposed on the new platform, so that customers' *other* vendors and internal systems don't all have to change on the same weekend.
- **Per-account parity certificate** — a finite, signed checklist: "these are the 14 things you rely on; here is the status and date of each." This is the highest-leverage artifact in the program. Unbounded anxiety becomes a list of fourteen items, and lists get closed.

---

## 6. Tiered migration and incentives

Sequencing note: I wouldn't do hardest-first *or* hardest-last. One or two hard accounts early, deliberately over-resourced, to prove it can be done and generate a reference. Then volume through the tail to harden the tooling. Complex accounts in the middle-to-late window, when the tooling has scar tissue.

**Tier A — Strategic (top ~20 accounts, the defection risks)**
Wave: T0+3 to T0+36. Named migration architect and executive sponsor per account. Migration services fully funded by us. Multi-year price lock and contract co-termination. Design-partner status with a real seat on the parity roadmap — influence is a more durable retention tool than money, and cheaper. A written parity guarantee with a remedy attached: if we miss a committed parity date, they get extended support at our cost until we don't. And a "no worse off" commitment: total cost of ownership held flat for 24 months post-migration.

**Tier B — Mid-market**
Wave: T0+12 to T0+36. Pooled migration engineers, scheduled migration windows, a migration credit (roughly one quarter of annual value) applied against services or the new subscription. Cohort-based onboarding — customers with similar configurations moved together, which is efficient for us and reassuring for them. Multi-year renewal incentive tied to migration completion.

**Tier C — Long tail / SMB**
Wave: T0+6 to T0+30. Self-service end to end: scanner, converter, guided in-product migration, community and documentation. Incentive is time-decaying — best terms in the first year, standard terms later, uplifted pricing after. Pure self-service migration should be measurably *better* than the assisted path, not a lesser version of it.

**Tier D — OEM / embedded / partners**
Often forgotten, frequently the messiest, because their own customers are downstream and their release cycles are long. Start earliest (T0+0), longest runway, joint roadmap alignment, and possibly a licensed compatibility layer they maintain themselves.

**Gate 2 (T0 + 18m):** honest read on migration velocity against the curve. If we're materially behind, the correction is scope and tooling — not the date. Moving the date once teaches everyone the date isn't real.

---

## 7. Retention plan for the likely defectors

**Read the threats carefully.** Some are leverage-seeking, timed to renewal, and will resolve with parity commitments and commercial protection. Some are real, usually where a new executive sponsor has arrived with a mandate, or where a competitor has already been let in the building. These need different responses, and conflating them wastes goodwill on the first group and time on the second. I'd want a per-account read on which is which before anyone offers anything.

**Early-warning score**, refreshed monthly: renewal date proximity, open parity gaps, competitor presence, sponsor turnover, support sentiment trend, integration depth (a proxy for real switching cost), usage trajectory, procurement signals (RFI activity, security questionnaires arriving from elsewhere).

**Sequencing with the top accounts.** Private, senior, one-to-one conversations *before* the public announcement — not to soften a blow, but to give them the parity roadmap, the tooling demo, and an offer of design-partner influence. The subtext writes itself: they find out early, with a plan and a seat at the table, rather than reading it on a blog. That distinction does more for retention than any discount schedule.

**On renewals:** the honest play is a migration-inclusive multi-year agreement — new platform commitment, legacy support through the transition, migration funded, parity guaranteed. Selling a legacy renewal while sitting on an unannounced EOL date is the one thing here that would genuinely destroy us if it surfaced, and it would surface.

**Make switching costs visible without being crude.** A migration to a competitor is *also* a migration — same data, same integrations, same retraining, same risk, minus a decade of accumulated configuration and minus us funding it. A neutral, factual side-by-side comparison of the two paths is persuasive precisely because it doesn't argue.

**Budget for loss, and be specific about it.** Something like: protect ≥90% of legacy revenue through EOL, with acceptable attrition concentrated in low-margin, low-strategic-fit accounts. Naming an acceptable loss prevents heroic, margin-destroying rescues of accounts we'd rather not have had. And for those who do leave: excellent data export, a graceful exit, no bitterness, and a standing 18-month win-back offer. A meaningful fraction come back once they've priced the alternative properly.

---

## 8. Team and governance

A small core — twelve or so — with one accountable owner and real decision rights: program lead, migration engineering, tooling, parity/product, customer success, commercial, plus the legacy engineering elders. Weekly working rhythm, monthly one-page signal to leadership. Two gates, as above. Beyond that I'd keep it out of committee — this program will need dozens of small judgement calls made quickly by whoever is closest to the customer, and every approval layer we add is a week of migration velocity we lose.

**Metrics that matter:** legacy revenue migrated (the headline), migration cycle time by tier, defection rate versus pre-program churn baseline, parity gaps open/closed, post-migration retention and expansion, legacy run cost and vulnerability exposure, cost per migrated account, and bus factor per legacy subsystem.

---

## 9. Where I think this breaks, and questions I'd deliberately leave open

Most likely failure modes: the parity list grows faster than we close it, because every account discovers a new dependency once they look; the announcement triggers a competitive evaluation wave we've under-resourced; a critical legacy CVE lands in year three with nobody left who can safely patch it; the migration engineering capacity gets quietly raided for new-product roadmap work; and — most probable of all — a date slips and the whole timeline loses its authority.

Three things I'd rather not resolve on paper yet, because the answers should come from Phase 0 data rather than from a meeting:

Whether the compatibility layer is a bridge or a permanent product. It may quietly become the latter, and that's not necessarily bad — but we should notice it happening rather than discover it.

Whether the irreducible bespoke core is small enough to serve, or large enough to divest. The triage table answers this, and I'd genuinely like to see the number before anyone forms a view.

And whether the loyalty of these customers is to the features, or to the fact that someone once built exactly what they asked for. If it's the second, no amount of parity engineering closes the gap — and the retention plan should look quite different.

# Margin Recovery Under Sustained Input Inflation
## A Portfolio Approach — Draft for Discussion, Not for Ratification

*A note on how I've built this: I've deliberately left several forks open rather than closing them, because the two blunt increases suggest the problem was never insufficient conviction — it was insufficient discrimination. What follows is a shape and a set of mechanisms. The specific settings should be chosen by whoever is closest to the data, and revised as the market answers back.*

---

## 1. What the Two Failed Increases Were Actually Telling Us

Before adding a third move, it may be worth sitting with what the first two produced. Two blunt increases, partially rejected, with volume falling faster than forecast in price-sensitive segments and one chain delisting three items — that's not a pricing failure so much as an **aggregation failure**. An average increase applied to a portfolio with heterogeneous elasticity will always over-price the elastic tail and under-price the inelastic core. The volume loss came from the former; the margin left on the table sits in the latter.

Four diagnostic questions I'd want answered in the first three weeks, because everything downstream depends on them:

| Question | Output required |
|---|---|
| What is our true **net-net margin by SKU × customer**? (After off-invoice, scan, billbacks, logistics allowances, slotting amortisation, returns, unsaleables) | A margin heat map. Expect 15–25% of SKU/customer combinations to be below variable-cost contribution. |
| What is **realised elasticity**, not modelled elasticity, per segment and per price tier? | Post-event elasticity read from the last two increases — this is a rare gift of clean data. Segment by brand tier, category, and shopper income proxy. |
| What is the **true competitive price gap** on a normalised basis? | Price-per-serving *and* price-per-unit-weight *and* shelf price, tracked alongside competitor pack-size and formulation changes. The muddying is a fact to be exploited, not merely endured. |
| What did the delisting actually cost — **and what did it cost the retailer**? | Our lost GM$ vs. their lost category sales, basket incidence, and switching data. This is negotiation currency. |

The last point deserves emphasis. Three delisted products are not purely a loss; they are an experiment someone else ran on our behalf. If the retailer's category sales in those subcategories fell, or shoppers substituted to a lower-margin item, or trips shifted, we now hold evidence we did not have before.

---

## 2. Framing: Six Points Do Not Come From One Lever

The instinct after a rejected increase is a larger increase. The arithmetic suggests otherwise. Rough shape of a bridge — illustrative magnitudes to be calibrated against the diagnostic:

| Lever | Gross GM points | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Net price realisation (surgical list + terms discipline + leakage) | +1.8 to 2.2 | Q1–Q3 |
| Price-pack architecture (entry packs, weight-out, premium tiers) | +0.8 to 1.2 | Q2–Q4 |
| Mix management (portfolio, channel, customer, tail cull) | +0.6 to 1.0 | Q1–Q5 |
| Trade promotion redesign (efficiency, not withdrawal) | +1.0 to 1.4 | Q2–Q4 |
| Cost engineering (formulation, packaging, network, complexity) | +1.2 to 1.8 | Q2–Q6 |
| **Gross recovery** | **+5.4 to 7.6** | |
| Less: volume/distribution drag | −0.8 to −1.5 | |
| **Net recovery** | **+4.5 to 6.0** | 6 quarters |

Two implications worth naming plainly. First, no single lever exceeds ~2 points, so no single lever needs to be pushed to the point where it breaks a customer relationship. Second, a portion may be structurally unrecoverable — if the category has permanently re-based, chasing the final point could cost more in distribution than it earns in margin. I'd rather bank 5.0 durable points than fight for 6.0 and lose a second retailer.

---

## 3. List Price: From Blunt to Surgical

**Replace the across-the-board increase with a tiered architecture.** Segment every SKU on two axes:

- **Pricing power**: brand equity, private-label price gap, distribution exclusivity, purchase-frequency/loyalty, share of shelf, substitutability.
- **Price exposure**: how visible and comparable the item is (destination/traffic-driver items, KVIs, items with direct competitor matches at identical size).

|  | **Low exposure** | **High exposure** |
|---|---|---|
| **High pricing power** | **Tier A — lead here.** +6 to 10%. Inelastic, low visibility. This is where the last two increases under-delivered. | **Tier B — hold or +2–3%.** Protect the price-gap optics. Recover margin here via pack and cost levers instead. |
| **Low pricing power** | **Tier C — +4 to 6%,** paired with cost engineering. Candidates for rationalisation if they don't respond. | **Tier D — do not raise list.** Recover via pack size, promo depth reduction, or exit. These are where volume fell faster than forecast. |

**Mechanics that reduce rejection risk:**

- **Smaller, more frequent moves.** Two 4% increases nine months apart absorb far better than one 8%. Frequency is the friend of realisation; magnitude is the enemy.
- **Respect psychological thresholds.** Never let a move push a shelf price through a round number. Where it would, use pack architecture instead and let the retailer keep the price point.
- **Cost-index linkage in the contract, not the conversation.** Propose a transparent pass-through mechanism tied to published indices (grain, dairy, resin, diesel, PPI energy) with a symmetric downside. This converts a recurring confrontation into an administrative process, and it is far easier for a buyer to accept a formula than an ask. It also removes the annual "prove it" ritual. Some will refuse; the ones who accept become your easier customers permanently.
- **Terms and leakage discipline.** Prompt-payment discounts, drop-size thresholds, pallet/case configurations, unsaleables allowances, new-item slotting amortisation. There is typically 50–120bps sitting here, invisible on the P&L and rarely defended by buyers because it isn't shelf price. I'd take this before I took list price.

---

## 4. Pack Architecture: The Lever Competitors Are Already Using

They are shrinking packs and reformulating precisely because it decouples our economics from the shelf price the shopper compares. Rather than complain about muddied comparisons, we might participate in the muddying with more discipline than they have.

**Build a deliberate ladder, differentiated by channel:**

| Channel | Pack role | Design intent |
|---|---|---|
| **Discount / value grocery** | **Entry price point (EPP)** — smaller count/weight at a defensible round shelf price | Protects trial and price-sensitive volume without touching core pricing. Higher margin per unit weight than the core. This is the direct answer to the volume loss. |
| **Conventional grocery** | Core mid-size, held at recognisable price points | Where price-gap optics matter most. Recover via cost engineering and modest weight-out, not list. |
| **Club / mass** | Large-count value packs, club-exclusive configurations | Non-comparable by design; margin per unit lower but fixed-cost absorption and mix contribution high. |
| **Convenience / immediate consumption** | Single-serve and portable formats | Highest margin per unit weight in the portfolio; systematically under-exploited by most packaged-food producers. |
| **E-commerce / DTC** | Ship-optimised multipacks, subscription bundles | Price per unit higher, comparison friction highest, first-party data on elasticity. Under-used as a pricing laboratory. |

**On weight-out — the decision to make consciously rather than by drift.** Reducing net content while holding shelf price is the most efficient margin lever available and the highest-reputation-risk one. Three postures, and I'd want the leadership team to choose one and not oscillate:

1. **Silent weight-out** — fastest, standard practice, carries backlash exposure and increasingly attracts regulatory and media attention in several markets.
2. **Weight-out paired with visible improvement** — new resealable closure, recyclable pack, reformulation upgrade, portion-control framing. Redirects the narrative from what was removed to what was added.
3. **Deliberate non-shrink as a claim** — hold size, raise price, and *say so*: "same size since [year]." A minority position, but if competitor shrink is as widespread as described, there is an asymmetric opportunity in being the brand that raised price honestly. It also plays unusually well in a retailer conversation.

My own inclination — and I'd hold it loosely — is (2) for the core and (3) for one or two flagship items where trust is the actual equity. Option (3) additionally gives the sales team something to say in a JBP meeting that no discount can substitute for.

**A tool worth building regardless:** a *true net price tracker* that normalises every competitor SKU for size and formulation change and shows the retailer what has actually happened to price-per-serving across the shelf over 18 months. Buyers are frequently blind to this. Arriving with it reframes us from supplicant to category adviser, and quietly reveals that our ask is below the market's realised move.

---

## 5. Mix Management: The Quietest Two Points

Margin can rise while every price stays still. Four mix layers:

- **Portfolio mix.** Rank SKUs by GM$ per unit of scarce capacity (line hours, shelf facings, distribution slots). Actively steer trade spend, innovation, and sales incentives toward the top quartile. Most sales incentive schemes reward volume or revenue; recasting them on GM$ changes behaviour faster than any directive.
- **Tail rationalisation.** A 15–25% SKU cull typically costs 3–6% of revenue and *adds* margin: fewer changeovers, longer runs, less obsolescence, lower working capital, better in-stock on the survivors. It is also a negotiation asset — cutting your own tail before a buyer does converts a defeat into a jointly-planned assortment optimisation. Note the sequencing: **propose your cull list before the buyer builds theirs.**
- **Premiumisation.** A credible better/best tier does more than earn its own margin; it raises the reference price for the core and gives the retailer a margin-accretive item to defend. Under sustained inflation, category polarisation is normal — value and premium grow, the middle hollows. Build for both ends.
- **Channel and customer mix.** Shift growth investment toward convenience, foodservice-adjacent, e-commerce, and independents where net-net margin is structurally higher and buying power lower. This reduces dependence on the chains that can delist us, which is the deeper problem the six points only symptomise.

---

## 6. Promotion Redesign: Spend Less, Buy More

Trade spend is usually the largest and least governed item on the P&L. In a category being tactically discounted to muddy comparisons, the temptation is to match. That's the trap: matching tactical discounts converts a competitor's temporary cost into our permanent price expectation.

**Diagnostic:** incremental ROI for every event over the last 24 months — incremental volume net of forward-buy, pantry-loading, cannibalisation, and post-event dip. Typical finding: 25–40% of events are ROI-negative, and a small number of well-supported events deliver most of the incremental volume.

**Redesign principles:**

1. **Reallocate, don't withdraw.** Cut the negative tail; redeploy roughly half the freed spend into the proven events and retain half as margin. Total spend down, incremental volume flat or up. This is the version a buyer can accept, because their key events survive.
2. **Fewer, better-supported events.** Depth plus display plus feature beats frequent shallow price-off. Reduce *frequency* first — frequency is what erodes the reference price and trains the shopper to wait.
3. **Convert unconditional to conditional.** Move off-invoice allowances toward scan-based/pay-for-performance with agreed execution compliance. Off-invoice money leaks into forward-buy and diversion; scan money buys actual shopper action. Expect resistance — this is a real transfer of value — so trade it for something.
4. **Personalise instead of publish.** Loyalty-card and retail-media targeted offers let us discount to the price-sensitive shopper *without* lowering the shelf price that everyone else sees and that competitors benchmark. This is the single most elegant answer to segment-level price sensitivity: keep the shelf price for the inelastic, deliver the discount only where it changes behaviour. Retailers have this infrastructure and are motivated to monetise it.
5. **Manage promoted price as carefully as list.** Cap maximum discount depth by SKU. A deep feature at a price point below the entry-pack economics silently destroys the pack architecture we just built.
6. **Kill price-comparison exposure on promotion.** Where possible, promote on multi-buy, bundle, or loyalty mechanics rather than single-unit price-off — harder to benchmark, less reference-price damage.

---

## 7. Cost Engineering: Targeted, Sequenced, Sensory-Guarded

Price alone cannot carry six points without volume damage. Roughly 25–30% of the recovery should come from cost, and it is the portion retailers respect most — because it is the portion where we are visibly sharing the burden rather than passing it on.

| Lever | Where the value sits | Guardrail |
|---|---|---|
| **Formulation / value engineering** | Ingredient substitution, yield improvement, functional-system redesign, spec tolerance | **Blind sensory testing against current product with a defined non-inferiority threshold.** Never ship a spec change that fails. A quality-driven repeat-rate decline costs more than the saving, and is invisible until it isn't. |
| **Packaging** | Lightweighting, resin/board downgauging, format change, secondary-pack elimination, pallet cube optimisation | Shelf-impact and damage-rate testing; sustainability narrative where genuine |
| **Freight & network** | Mode shift, drop-size incentives, backhaul, load consolidation, regional co-pack to shorten lanes, dedicated-fleet vs. spot mix, cube-fill improvement | Service level to key customers must not degrade during a price negotiation — in-stock is the retailer's currency |
| **Complexity reduction** | Fewer SKUs → longer runs, fewer changeovers, less obsolescence, simpler forecasting | Follows the tail cull; capture the saving explicitly rather than letting it dissipate |
| **Procurement** | Index-linked contracts, dual sourcing, structured hedging with a stated policy, supplier-led VA/VE programmes, should-cost modelling | Hedge to reduce volatility, not to speculate; publish the policy so it isn't re-litigated each quarter |
| **Energy & conversion** | Utility efficiency capex, OEE, scrap/waste/giveaway reduction, line speed | Fast payback projects first; keep a live list of <18-month-payback items |

**Sequencing note:** launch cost engineering *before* the next price conversation, not after. Being able to say "we have already taken X million out of our own cost base" changes the character of the discussion entirely. It is also the honest position — and the one hardest to argue with.

---

## 8. Differentiation Across Channels and Segments

The core insight from the failed increases: one price move cannot serve a portfolio serving very different shoppers.

| Segment / channel | Price posture | Pack | Promotion | Primary margin lever |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Loyal / brand-committed shoppers** (measured by repeat rate, not demographics) | Full increase, Tier A | Core & premium | Minimal; protect reference price | List price |
| **Price-sensitive / trade-down risk** | No list increase on exposed items | **Entry price-point pack** at a held shelf price | Targeted loyalty offers only | Pack architecture + cost |
| **Conventional grocery chains** | Modest list; heavy emphasis on cost-sharing story and assortment optimisation | Core sizes, held price points | Fewer, deeper, better-executed | Promo efficiency + mix |
| **Discount / limited-assortment** | Everyday-low, no promo; simplified spec | EPP and value formats | None | Cost engineering, complexity reduction |
| **Club / warehouse** | Item-level value; accept lower GM% for GM$ and absorption | Large-count exclusives | Roadshows / MVM only | Volume-driven absorption; non-comparable packs |
| **Convenience / immediate consumption** | Full increase; least price-sensitive occasion | Single-serve | Rare | Highest margin per unit weight in portfolio |
